```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r libraries}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(tibble)
library(scales)
```

```{r load-texts}
file_a <- "A07594__Circle_of_Commerce.txt"
file_b <- "B14801__Free_Trade.txt"

text_a <- read_file(file_a)
text_b <- read_file(file_b)

texts <- tibble(
  doc_title = c("Text A", "Text B"),
  text = c(text_a, text_b)
)

texts
```

```{r stopword-lists}
data("stop_words")

custom_stopwords <- tibble(
  word = c(
    "vnto", "haue", "doo", "hath", "bee", "ye", "thee"
  )
)

all_stopwords <- bind_rows(stop_words, custom_stopwords) %>%
  distinct(word)
```


## Part I: Diagnostics table

```{r words-tokenized}
# Tokenize WITHOUT removing stopwords yet
words <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  mutate(word = str_to_lower(word))
```

```{r corpus-diagnostics}
corpus_diagnostics <- words %>%
  count(doc_title, name = "total_tokens") %>%
  left_join(
    words %>%
      anti_join(all_stopwords, by = "word") %>%
      count(doc_title, name = "tokens_after_stopwords"),
    by = "doc_title"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    tokens_removed  = total_tokens - tokens_after_stopwords,
    percent_removed = round(100 * tokens_removed / total_tokens, 1)
  )

corpus_diagnostics
```

### Interpretive questions for Section I

- What percentage of each document was removed as stopwords?
- Is the percentage approximately the same for the two documents?
- What do these numbers tell you about how substantially stopword removal has transformed the texts you'll be analyzing?

**Answer:**

Text A had 56.6% removed, and Text B had 59.8% removed. The two percentages are close, within about 3 percentage points, so I would assume stop-word removal affects both texts similarly, even though Text A is a lot longer overall (33,894 tokens compared to 19,924), the proportion taken up by other words is fairly comparable.From the list of stopwords removed, we can assume that both texts utilise a lot of function words.


## Part II: Most frequent words before vs. after stopword removal

### A. Before stopword removal

```{r before-counts}
word_counts_before <- words %>%
  count(doc_title, word, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r before-plot}
plot_n_words <- 15

word_comparison_before <- word_counts_before %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = doc_title,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(max_n = pmax(`Text A`, `Text B`)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_n))

word_plot_data_before <- word_comparison_before %>%
  slice_head(n = plot_n_words) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Text A`, `Text B`),
    names_to = "doc_title",
    values_to = "n"
  ) %>%
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n, .fun = max))

ggplot(word_plot_data_before, aes(x = n, y = word)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ doc_title, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent words before stopword removal",
    x = "Word frequency",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### B. After stopword removal

```{r after-counts}
words_clean <- words %>%
  anti_join(all_stopwords, by = "word")

word_counts_after <- words_clean %>%
  count(doc_title, word, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r after-plot}
word_comparison_after <- word_counts_after %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = doc_title,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(max_n = pmax(`Text A`, `Text B`)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_n))

word_plot_data_after <- word_comparison_after %>%
  slice_head(n = plot_n_words) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Text A`, `Text B`),
    names_to = "doc_title",
    values_to = "n"
  ) %>%
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n, .fun = max))

ggplot(word_plot_data_after, aes(x = n, y = word)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ doc_title, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent words after stopword removal",
    x = "Word frequency",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Interpretive questions for Section II

- What dominates the frequency results before stopword removal?
- What becomes visible after stopword removal?
- Does removing stopwords make it easier to say something about the subject matter of these texts? Give at least two specific examples from your results.
- What information about the texts becomes less visible when we remove stopwords?

**Answer:**

Function words, like "the", "of", "and" and "in", dominated both texts before stopword removal. After stopword removal, we can see that Text A has far more content words, "trade", "money", and "kingdome", remaining, which makes sense given that Text A had many more tokens to begin with. These content words make it far more easier to deduce what the texts focus on.

I also notice what looks like a special character for s, in which these words are featured frequently in Text A, but not present at all in Text B. This might indicate the age or age of content in each text.

In Text A, after stopword removal, the word "malynes", likely from the english economist, becomes very frequent. This reveals his significant presence in the subject matter of the text.

From what I can see, I'm not sure that we lose any valuable content/information through the stopword removal step.


## Part III: Testing the custom stopword list

```{r partial-stopwords}
words_partial <- words %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

word_counts_partial <- words_partial %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

word_comparison_partial <- words_partial %>%
  count(doc_title, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = doc_title,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(max_n = pmax(`Text A`, `Text B`)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_n))

top15_partial <- word_comparison_partial %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

top15_partial
```

### Interpretive question for Section III

- Identify at least three words whose presence helps explain why the custom stopword list was created.
- Why might these words be unhelpful if the goal is to identify the subject matter of the documents?
- Can you imagine a research question for which one of these words would be useful evidence?
- Based on this experiment, explain why there is no single, universally "correct" stopword list.

**Answer:**
From the comparison table, we can see "haue", "hath", "bee", and "ye" from our original stopword list, are all in the top 15. When trying to identify the content of the texts, these words do no do much to make it clear, rather function more as articles and prepositions. A research question we might be able to answer using the most frequent words, is the time period a text was written. From this experiment, comparing even just the two texts provided, there is no universal stopword list that would be transferable between texts since even texts with the same subject matter utilize words differently. Some words are used more commonly in one text, while others carry different meaning that may or may not be significant and useful depending on the text.


## Final Reflection

*(In 3-5 sentences, respond to the following statement, using at least one specific result from your analysis as evidence:) "Stopword removal is just data cleaning. It doesn't affect the interpretation because we are only removing unimportant words." *

**Answer:**
Stopword removal, cannot predict that all words removed are unimportant. Since stopwords are often the most common words featured in a text, if we were to simply remove the most common words every time we applied stopword removal, in the example of Text A, we might miss out on "malynes" who is directly relevant to the subject matter. Even part II exemplifies how the choice of stopword removal can influence what question can/ should be interrogated from the remaining tokens.
